title: What does the evidence say about titanium in people?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: Systemic titanium from implants or from E171
grade.basis: The food-additive conclusion is one EFSA opinion. The implant evidence is three small human series without a clinical outcome.

answerHtml: EFSA in 2021 said a concern for genotoxicity of titanium dioxide (E171) could not be ruled out, and that E171 could no longer be considered safe as a food additive. Three small human studies found higher serum titanium in people with hip or spinal implants than in comparison groups. None of those studies measured a systemic health outcome from the titanium.

sections.heading: Food additive E171
sections.html: The corpus records two statements as checked against the EFSA 2021 opinion: a concern for genotoxicity could not be ruled out, and E171 can no longer be considered safe as a food additive. A statement that no acceptable daily intake was set was marked unverified and is not repeated. EFSA 2021. An IARC classification for titanium dioxide was not opened and is not stated.

sections.heading: Implants
sections.html:
Omlor and colleagues (2013) measured 67 patients and compared them with 11 people with non-modular implants and 23 people without implants. Both implant groups had higher serum titanium. The abstract called the absolute levels comparatively low. No systemic health outcome was measured. doi:10.1016/j.actbio.2012.12.001.

Cundy and colleagues (2014) followed 33 children with titanium-alloy spinal fusion. More than 95 percent of postoperative serum titanium and niobium levels were elevated, and levels correlated with implant surface area. Clinical implications were described as uncertain. doi:10.1007/s00586-014-3279-x.

Kasai and colleagues (2003) compared 46 spinal-implant patients with 20 controls. About one third had abnormal serum or hair metal values. Serum levels did not indicate implant failure. doi:10.1097/01.BRS.0000065482.41115.B4.

There is no validated clinical reference range for titanium in this corpus, and the CDC National Report list used here has no titanium table.
